extracted.intended_audience: short fiction authors submitting to Clarkesworld and SFF writers interested in editorial perspective
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial guidance and observations about story titles in short speculative-fiction submissions to Clarkesworld, focusing on how titles affect (or don't affect) acceptance and trends. Includes simple statistics about duplicate titles and notes on how submission policy affects title word frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: title_not_a_basis_for_rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: I have never rejected a story because it had a common (or even a terrible) title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a common or 'bad' title will cause automatic rejection. Editors may dismiss or dislike a title but will judge the story on its merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: title_not_considered_before_purchase
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t give any thought to the title before I’ve decided to purchase a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial purchase decisions are based on the story itself; titles are generally irrelevant to the initial buying decision and are secondary to content and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: titles_can_be_changed_post_acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing a title is easy, so if I don’t like it, I can have that discussion with the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors need not be overly attached to a submitted title — editors can and will negotiate or suggest title changes after acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: title_not_indicator_of_story_quality
rubrics_metrics.description: There are plenty of good stories and bad stories with those titles. The title is not what made them good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong title does not guarantee a strong story and vice versa; invest primary effort in narrative, craft, and execution rather than relying on title to carry the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: duplicate_title_statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplicated titles represent a small minority—less than 10%—of all submissions to Clarkesworld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique titles are the norm; while some titles recur, most submissions have distinct titles. Authors can expect that title duplication is relatively uncommon.

rubrics_metrics.name: duplicate_titles_excluding_articles
rubrics_metrics.description: It doesn't even pass 20% when you remove all the common variations that come by adding the, an, a, etc. to the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring title uniqueness, account for trivial variations like articles; even when those are normalized, duplicates remain a minority.

rubrics_metrics.name: common_title_trends_change_over_time
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the first report, we have three new titles breaking into the top ten: The Interview, First Contact, and The Visitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title popularity shifts over submission cohorts; authors should not assume a title's commonness is permanent—trends evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: submission_policy_affects_title_word_frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: “Zombies” made the cut. I’ve previously told you they were everywhere in the slush pile. Now that we’re not accepting horror submissions, maybe that will fall off the list...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magazine submission policies (e.g., not accepting horror) will change the frequency of certain title words. Authors should consult current guidelines for genre restrictions, which affect what editors see in the slush pile.

rubrics_metrics.name: editorial_data_is_informal_and_for_interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike previous data-based editorials, this was done strictly for the fun of it. The only statistic worth noting this time, is that duplicated titles represent a small minority—less than 10%...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statistics and analyses presented are informal, anecdotal, and intended as editorial insight rather than prescriptive submission rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: word_frequency_visualization_top_title_words
rubrics_metrics.description: I took every story title ever received by Clarkesworld and dropped it into Wordle to produce the following visual representation of the top 150 words used in titles (minus the common English-language words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualizations (word clouds) of title-word frequency can reveal common themes and recurring words; authors can use such data to spot trends but should prioritize original, story-appropriate titles.
